hints: Hint 1: Focus on the word active. Ask yourself, who makes the antibodies in active immunity, you (self) or someone else (non-self)?
Hint 2: Artificially induced means vaccination, so a harmless non-self antigen is put in. Remember the golden rule: antibodies attack antigens, antigens never attack antibodies.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Sort out active versus passive**
Active immunity means your own immune system does the work. Your B lymphocytes are activated and your plasma cells make your own (self) antibodies. This is slow but gives long term memory.

Passive immunity is the opposite, you are given ready made (non-self) antibodies from someone else.

Step 2: **Add in artificially induced**
Artificially just means by human intervention, which is vaccination. A vaccine contains non-self antigens, for example weakened pathogen or isolated antigen, to stimulate you without causing disease.

Step 3: **Put it together and check direction**
So you make self antibodies in response to the vaccine non-self antigens. And always remember, antibodies are the weapons that attack antigens, not the other way round.

That gives: Self antibodies attack non-self antigens, which is option C.

options.A: This describes passive immunity, where you receive non-self antibodies made by another organism. It also wrongly suggests attack on self, which would be autoimmunity.
options.B: The direction is backwards. Antigens do not attack antibodies, antibodies bind to and attack antigens.
options.C: Correct. In artificial active immunity (vaccination), non-self vaccine antigens stimulate your body to make its own self antibodies against them, plus memory cells.
options.D: This is backwards twice. Your self antigens are your own cell markers, and antigens never attack antibodies.
